title: Fourier Series: Building a Wave
intro: Any repeating signal is a sum of sinusoids whose frequencies are multiples of the repeat rate. The recipe for how much of each one is a single integral, and it works because different harmonics are orthogonal.

blocks.text: The claim

Let $x(t)$ repeat every $T$ seconds. Call $f_0 = 1/T$ its fundamental frequency and $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$ the angular version. The claim of Fourier's series is that $x(t)$ is a sum of turning arrows at $0, \pm f_0, \pm 2f_0, \ldots$:

blocks.tex: x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k\, e^{jk\omega_0 t}, \qquad c_k = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x(t)\, e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\, dt

blocks.text: The numbers $c_k$ are complex: $|c_k|$ is the length of the $k$th arrow and $\angle c_k$ its starting angle. The second formula says how to find them. For a real signal $c_{-k} = \overline{c_k}$, and each pair of arrows $c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} + c_{-k}e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$ combines into one real cosine, as the Sinusoids and Complex Exponentials (#/math/fourier-transform/sinusoids) page showed. That gives the form the viewer uses:

blocks.tex: x(t) = A_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k\cos(k\omega_0 t + \varphi_k), \qquad A_0 = c_0,\quad A_k = 2|c_k|,\quad \varphi_k = \angle c_k

blocks.text: The factor of 2 appears because the amplitude $A_k$ is shared between the two arrows $\pm k$. The $k = 0$ term is the average value of the signal, which has no negative partner. The $k$th term is the $k$th harmonic; $k = 1$ is the fundamental.
Why the integral finds the coefficient

The coefficient formula rests on one fact: different harmonics are orthogonal, meaning that multiplying two of them together and averaging over a period gives zero. Take the period $T = 1$ for simplicity. Then

blocks.tex: \int_0^1 e^{j2\pi k t}\, e^{-j2\pi m t}\, dt = \int_0^1 e^{j2\pi (k-m) t}\, dt

blocks.text: If $k = m$ the integrand is 1 and the integral is 1. If $k \ne m$, say $k - m = 2$, then

because $e^{j4\pi} = 1$: two whole turns bring the arrow home. Any nonzero whole number of turns does the same. So averaging $e^{jk\omega_0 t}e^{-jm\omega_0 t}$ over a period kills everything except $k = m$.

Now multiply the series by $e^{-jm\omega_0 t}$ and average over a period. Every term on the right averages to zero except the one with $k = m$, which averages to $c_m$. So $\frac1T\int_0^T x(t)e^{-jm\omega_0 t}dt = c_m$, which is the coefficient formula. In words: to find how much of frequency $m f_0$ is in a signal, spin the signal backwards at that frequency and take the average. If the signal contains that frequency, it stands still under the spin and the average is its size; every other component keeps turning and averages away.
The square wave
Take the square wave of the viewer with $T = 1$: $x = +1$ for $0 < t < \tfrac12$ and $-1$ for $\tfrac12 < t < 1$. Its average is zero, so $c_0 = 0$. For $k \ne 0$ split the integral:

blocks.tex: c_k = \int_0^{1/2} e^{-j2\pi k t}\,dt - \int_{1/2}^{1} e^{-j2\pi k t}\,dt = \frac{1 - e^{-j\pi k}}{j2\pi k} - \frac{e^{-j\pi k} - 1}{j2\pi k} = \frac{1 - (-1)^k}{j\pi k}

blocks.text: using $e^{-j\pi k} = (-1)^k$ and $e^{-j2\pi k} = 1$. For even $k$ this is 0. For odd $k$ it is $2/(j\pi k) = -j\,2/(\pi k)$. So $c_1 = -0.6366j$, $c_3 = -0.2122j$, $c_5 = -0.1273j$, and in amplitude-phase form

blocks.tex: A_k = \frac{4}{\pi k}\ \ (k \text{ odd}), \qquad \varphi_k = -90^\circ, \qquad x(t) = \frac{4}{\pi}\left[\sin\omega_0 t + \frac{\sin 3\omega_0 t}{3} + \frac{\sin 5\omega_0 t}{5} + \cdots\right]

blocks.text: since $\cos(\theta - 90^\circ) = \sin\theta$. A flat-topped wave is made entirely of odd harmonics, each one a third, a fifth, a seventh of the fundamental's strength. A numerical integral of $x(t)e^{-j2\pi k t}$ over one period confirms $c_1 = -0.6366j$, $c_2 = 0$ and $c_3 = -0.2122j$.

Press Add harmonics, or drag Harmonics added upward one at a time. N = 1 gives a smooth hump; N = 3 adds a second ribbon, one third as tall, and the sum starts to flatten; at N = 7 only four ribbons have any height, because the even ones are flat and the readout leaves them out. The right-hand wall shows bars of height 1.273, 0.424, 0.255 and so on, which is $4/\pi k$.
The sawtooth

The widget's sawtooth climbs from $-1$ to $+1$ over $-\tfrac12 < t < \tfrac12$, that is $x(t) = 2t$, then drops. Its average is 0, and for $k \ne 0$ integration by parts, $\int t\, e^{-jat}dt = \frac{t\, e^{-jat}}{-ja} + \frac{1}{ja}\int e^{-jat}dt$ with $a = 2\pi k$, gives

blocks.tex: c_k = 2\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} t\, e^{-j2\pi k t}\,dt = 2\cdot\frac{\cos(\pi k)}{-j2\pi k} = \frac{j(-1)^k}{\pi k}

blocks.text: The second part of the parts formula integrates $e^{-jat}$ over a whole number of turns, which is zero. So $c_1 = -0.3183j$, $c_2 = +0.1592j$, $c_3 = -0.1061j$: every harmonic is present, falling as $1/k$, with alternating phase. In amplitude form, $A_k = 2/(\pi k)$, and
The triangle wave, by calculus

The triangle wave $x(t) = 1 - 4|t|$ on $-\tfrac12 < t < \tfrac12$ goes from $+1$ at the centre to $-1$ at the ends. Integrating it directly is tedious; differentiating is easy. The slope is $-4$ for $t > 0$ and $+4$ for $t < 0$, so $x'(t) = -4s(t)$ where $s(t)$ is the square wave above. Differentiating a series multiplies each arrow by its $jk\omega_0$, so $c_k(x') = jk\omega_0\, c_k(x)$. Hence

blocks.tex: c_k(x) = \frac{c_k(x')}{j2\pi k} = \frac{-4\cdot 2/(j\pi k)}{j2\pi k} = \frac{-8}{j^2\, 2\pi^2 k^2} = \frac{4}{\pi^2 k^2}\quad (k \text{ odd})

blocks.text: so $A_k = 8/(\pi^2 k^2)$ with phase 0: $c_1 = 0.4053$, $c_3 = 0.0450$. The triangle has the same odd harmonics as the square wave, but they fall as $1/k^2$ instead of $1/k$. The harmonic at $k = 3$ is a ninth of the fundamental, not a third. The Convergence and the Gibbs Phenomenon (#/math/fourier-transform/convergence) page explains why a smoother wave has faster-falling coefficients.

Practice

blocks.title: Read a series
blocks.text: Find $c_k$ for $x(t) = 1 + 2\cos(2\pi t) + \sin(6\pi t)$, period 1.
solution: Write each term as arrows. $1$ is $c_0 = 1$. $2\cos(2\pi t) = e^{j2\pi t} + e^{-j2\pi t}$, so $c_1 = c_{-1} = 1$. $\sin(6\pi t) = (e^{j6\pi t} - e^{-j6\pi t})/2j$, so $c_3 = 1/(2j) = -0.5j$ and $c_{-3} = +0.5j$. Everything else is 0. In amplitude form, $A_0 = 1$, $A_1 = 2$ (phase 0), $A_3 = 1$ (phase $-90^\circ$).

blocks.title: A rectangular pulse train
blocks.text: A signal with period 1 is 1 for $|t| < 0.25$ and 0 for $0.25 < |t| < 0.5$. Find $c_0$ and $c_k$.
solution: $c_0$ is the average, $0.5$. For $k \ne 0$: $c_k = \int_{-0.25}^{0.25} e^{-j2\pi k t}dt = \frac{e^{-j\pi k/2} - e^{j\pi k/2}}{-j2\pi k} = \frac{\sin(\pi k/2)}{\pi k}$. For $k = 1$ that is $1/\pi = 0.3183$, for $k = 2$ it is 0, for $k = 3$ it is $-1/(3\pi) = -0.1061$. In amplitude form $A_1 = 0.6366$, $A_3 = 0.2122$ with phase $180^\circ$ (a negative $c_k$ is a phase of $\pi$). This is the pulse train in the viewer at $T = 1$.

blocks.title: Check orthogonality
blocks.text: With $T = 1$, compute $\int_0^1 \cos(2\pi t)\cos(6\pi t)\,dt$ and $\int_0^1\cos^2(2\pi t)\,dt$.
solution: Use $\cos a\cos b = \tfrac12[\cos(a-b) + \cos(a+b)]$. The first integral is $\tfrac12\int_0^1[\cos 4\pi t + \cos 8\pi t]\,dt = 0$, since each cosine completes whole cycles. The second is $\tfrac12\int_0^1[1 + \cos 4\pi t]\,dt = \tfrac12$. That is why a real cosine of amplitude $A$ contributes $A^2/2$ to the average power.
